China's Inflection Point Could Be Here 

(First published on Sparta's Market Outlook on 21 August, and point number 8 is already happening, with FOB premiums going up and eroding the cracking margins)

1⃣At least 8 mb of Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy cargoes have been sold to Rongsheng and some state-owned Chinese refiners for prompt delivery, with Basrah Medium rumoured to be at CFR Dubai + sub 10$/bbl levels.

2⃣This is apparently in reaction to missing out on the eighth ADNOC tender (they probably tried to bid for cheaper cargoes but failed).

3⃣Pre-crisis, from Sparta’s rolling front month arbs, the delivered pricing of Basrah Medium spot cargoes was around $2/bbl lower than Oman cargoes into Far East. With Oman currently landing around Oct Dubai+$19/bbl, the pricing of Basrah Medium at CFR Dubai+$10/bbl sounds reasonable.

4⃣On the Saudi allocations front, the quantity allocated to China is now heard to be 14 mb, just 1-2 VLCCs higher than the last three months of 10-12 mb allocations. Zhenhua was heard to have been allocated as well, signalling the start-up of the 300 kb/d HAPCO refinery is imminent.

5⃣There was also 10 mb of Arab Medium and Arab Heavy crudes heard sold on a rare Saudi Aramco tender to Petrochina, Sinochem, Unipec and Rong Sheng for prompt loading.

6⃣Russian ESPO is heard to be sold out for October loaders, whilst Iranian offers are few and far between for the independent refiners.

7⃣As a result, traders are seeing more active inquiries from both state-owned players and independent refiners.

 8⃣This should translate to higher achievable FOB premiums, given cracking margins are still in double digits in the Asian markets even with eye-watering freight rates.

9⃣Product exports could start creeping up around October if the crude buying pattern is sustained as well. We will of course need to hear the actual refined product export quotas to confirm.

#oott

An Important Week for U.S.-Iran Relations

This could be a consequential week for U.S.-Iran relations.

Washington is trying to intensify economic pressure on Tehran while finding operational workarounds that have allowed at least some oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz to return to global markets. At the same time, diplomatic efforts to bring the two sides back toward the framework of the earlier agreement appear to be gaining momentum.

The visit of Pakistan’s Army Chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, together with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s conversations with regional officials, suggests that all sides, and particularly the mediators, understand just how unstable the current situation is.

Meanwhile, the rhetoric coming out of Tehran is becoming increasingly threatening. Senior Iranian officials are making clear that Iran will not indefinitely tolerate a situation in which it cannot export its own oil while neighboring states continue exporting theirs, and, from Tehran’s perspective, cooperate with Washington in tightening the economic pressure on Iran.

The key question is what happens if Iran concludes that its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz is being eroded.

One possibility is that the growing pressure strengthens President Pezeshkian and others who favor additional compromises, potentially allowing Tehran to return to the previous framework without imposing new conditions.

But the opposite scenario is equally important. Iran may conclude that President Trump has little appetite for another major war ahead of the midterm elections, particularly given concerns over U.S. interceptor stockpiles. If so, Tehran could see military escalation not as a last resort, but as an increasingly attractive way to restore deterrence and leverage.

The increasingly aggressive statements from Iranian officials suggest that this option is very much under consideration. This matters even more because Iran’s strategic doctrine appears to be changing: Tehran is becoming more proactive, risk-tolerant, and willing to use offensive military action rather than simply absorb pressure and respond cautiously.

The central problem on the diplomatic front is that Washington, at least publicly, is offering Tehran no clear off-ramp. The administration appears to assume that sufficient economic pressure will eventually force Iranian capitulation. Statements by senior U.S. officials suggesting that economic pressure could even contribute to the regime’s collapse only make the mediators’ task more difficult.

So the real question this week is straightforward: Will the erosion of Iran’s position in the Strait push Tehran toward compromise, or toward escalation?

Could Iran accept a return to the previous framework without additional demands, or even show some flexibility over its control of the Strait? Or will greater pressure produce exactly the opposite effect, convincing Tehran that it needs to escalate in order to restore its leverage?

One thing increasingly appears clear: Iran is unlikely to accept the current status quo for long.

The intense diplomatic activity by regional mediators reflects precisely that concern. And given the low probability that Tehran will make the kind of far-reaching concessions Washington appears to expect, failure of the current diplomatic effort could bring the United States and Iran back toward military confrontation sooner than many anticipate.

Chokepoint traffic holds, risks shift

#MarineTraffic data show vessel traffic remained active through Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb last week, although headline volumes mask significant changes in the underlying mix. Hormuz recorded 121 crossings, up 2.5% from 118. Laden crossings fell 27% to 35, while ballast movements rose to 61 and sanctioned crossings increased from 9 to 16. Iran’s unilateral routing scheme accounted for 46.3% of crossings.

Bab el-Mandeb recorded 269 crossings, up 3.1% and roughly 2.2 times Hormuz volumes. Laden transits increased to 131, while dark transits fell from 23 to 15.
The figures show why vessel-level tracking matters when assessing changing maritime risk.

Oil experts are an interesting breed of people.  They are sorta like gold bugs.  For long periods they sit in a distant corner of the financial markets.  We pass by their desks and they nod at us and occasionally they get our attention and draw us close.  We hear their predictions of chaos and global doom.  We slowly back away and go about our business and live life. 

Episodically once every decade or so these same people are thrust to the center of the stage.  They haven't changed. They are the same people. It's us who have decided to pay attention.  Their story remains the same.  Energy is a physical commodity and real supply shocks will unleash chaos on the global economy for years to come.  The thing is they amaze us with their depth and understanding of all things energy.  Barrel count, geopolitical alignments of countries, grades, distillates, etc.  So many facts. So much depth.  So credible.  They always had this level of credibility.  They have specialized in this topic for their lifetime and we are simply tourists.  They are incredibly valuable and always have been.

Maybe this time is different.  Certainly market prices of oil and scarce immediate supply is "chaotic" and feeds back into the real economy.  Heck I care about the path of oil and its impact on the global economy and various market sectors.  At the same time I suggest recognizing that YOU are the one who has changed.  If your Oil guru or gurus have been saying the same thing for decades despite being wrong for decades it's your job to find the rare one who is pivoting and see their rationale and then for YOU to back slowly away from the perma oil bulls.

Gold options: Of the ten most actively traded COMEX gold option strikes over the past five sessions, nine are calls, highlighting the strong upside focus that has accompanied gold’s latest advance. The September C4,700, which expires later this week, tops the list, followed by the October C5,200 and C4,750. Further out, activity is also notable in December C5,500 and C6,000 calls, where open interest has risen to 14,469 and 17,603 contracts respectively. While option volume alone does not reveal whether these positions represent outright bullish bets, hedges or option-spread strategies, the concentration of activity in calls - particularly at strikes well above the current gold price near USD 4,730 - underlines elevated demand for upside exposure and protection against a further extension of the rally.

COT on US Treasury bond futures: 
Ahead of the US Treasury buyback announcement, there was no clear directional trend in speculative positioning across US Treasury futures. Speculators - defined here as the combined Leveraged Funds and Other Reportables categories - remained heavily short across the longer maturities, but changes during the latest reporting week were mixed.

Most notably, speculators sold a net 43k contracts of 10-year T-Notes, lifting the combined net short to 2.09 million contracts. In risk terms, this remains a substantial position, with a one-basis-point move in the underlying yield representing around USD 130 million in value, or DV01.

At the long end, the opposite occurred. Speculators bought around 30k contracts of 30-year T-Bonds, reducing the net short to 362k contracts. Despite the smaller contract position, its longer duration translates into a sizeable DV01 of around USD 47 million.

The largest speculative exposure in duration-adjusted terms remains the 30-year Ultra T-Bond, where the net short stood at 867k contracts, equivalent to a DV01 of around USD 141 million. Together with the sizeable 10-year T-Note short, this highlights the significant bearish duration exposure that was still in place immediately ahead of the Treasury announcement.

Importantly, these positions should not be viewed as outright, or "naked", directional shorts. A potentially sizeable share is likely linked to basis trades and relative-value strategies, including spreads against cash Treasuries, other maturities and corporate debt. As a result, the DV01 figures measure the interest-rate sensitivity of the futures leg rather than the expected profit or loss from an outright move in yields, as gains or losses may be partly or largely offset by positions elsewhere in the trade.
